newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar falls again, seen on brink of further dive.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls again, seen on brink of further dive.

text.p: The dollar fell to its lowest level against the yen since January in Asian trade on Thursday and Tokyo dealers said it appeared set to drop even further in the near term.
The dollar fell to around 115.60 yen in morning trade, down nearly 10 percent from a peak of 127.47 yen on May 1.

It was the dollar's lowest level since January 13 and dealers said the greenback could fall even further given a widespread belief in the market that both Japan and the United States are willing see a weaker U.S. currency to avoid renewed trade friction.
Dealers said Japanese trust banks had already carried out several billion dollars worth of dollar sales on behalf of corporate and public pension funds and more were set to follow.

"There are more who must hurry to sell dollars. You can't predict how far the dollar will fall before examining the magnitude of their sales," said Koichi Kubo, assistant general manager of the forex group at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd.
"The situation has completely turned in favour of dollar sales," said Ichiro Ikeda, director of the foreign exchange department at Credit Suisse First Boston in Tokyo.
"The dollar's fall is likely to overshoot the key 115 yen level in the near term."
A senior official at one trust bank estimated Japanese trust banks could sell off another five or six billion dollars, should the greenback fall to 110 yen.
"Our corporate pension fund customers tend to sell dollars for hedging or to dump foreign assets automatically when the dollar breaks through the certain levels," he said.

A senior trader at another trust bank said pension funds were reluctant to wait for the dollar to rebound before making hedge sales. "What they are doing is to trying to avoid the worst case by fixing profits or losses."
At its lowest point on Thursday, the dollar was almost two yen below its level in late U.S. trading on Wednesday. It recovered somewhat to around 116.20 yen by late afternoon.
Dealers said the next levels that would prompt fresh rounds of panic sales would be 115 and 113 yen.
Sales by the trust banks have exaggerated the speed of the dollar's drop and dealers said there was a risk of an even steeper fall if life insurance firms and exporters follow suit.
"Life insurers and exporters which have been relaxed about dollar sales were puzzled by the steep tumble this week," said a dealer at a European bank.

Dealers said some Japanese insurers have kept buying the dollar on its way down to 117 yen from 123 yen in a bid to lower the cost of their average dollar positions. However, such a strategy could backfire if the dollar falls below 115 yen.
A manager at a life insurance firm said the breakeven point for his company's foreign investments would be around 115 yen.

Asked about the recent movements in the currency market, influential Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara told reporters that they showed that an agreement last month between the Group of Seven nations on currencies had sufficiently filtered through the markets.

Sakakibara, known as Mr Yen for the influence he wields in currency markets, declined to comment when asked if the pace of the dollar's fall was too rapid and when asked what the impact would be on the Japanese economy.
Some dealers said they were waiting for a speech by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin later on Thursday.
"I think Rubin will stay quiet over the dollar's recent falls, since U.S. currency policy is not short-term orientated like that of Japan," said Credit Suisse's Ikeda.

Analysts said that as long as U.S. financial markets were stable and inflation was kept under control, the United States would be happy with the dollar's decline since this would prevent its trade deficit with Japan from increasing.
